transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-15 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 47m
Location: Zoom
Recording: available
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Maya (Calyx - Head of MLOps), Jon Lopez (CTO), Priya (SRE)

Summary:
Quick triage of week-3 POC benchmarks vs their incumbent provider. Focus on tail latency spikes, throughput plateau at 250 req/s, and variance under mixed batch sizes. Decide next tuning steps: KV-cache warmup, quantization profile, and dedicated slot increase for peak windows.

Links shared: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/calyx-week3 (bench csv), https://drive.company/calyx-logs (endpoint logs), Security appendix: https://redwood.app/docs/security/soc2-appendix.pdf

Topics covered:
- Latency vs baseline (p50/p95/p99)
- Throughput plateau and contention at 250 req/s
- KV-cache hit rates and prefix caching behavior
- Quantization tradeoffs for 8-bit vs 4-bit on customer workloads
- Next steps: extra dedicated slots, quantization deep-dive, security docs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for joining. um, quick roll call?
[00:05] Maya: maya here. jon on in a bit, priya's on.
[00:10] Jon: hey guys, sorry was on another call. we ran the overnight tests, good to sync.
[00:18] Ravi: cool, i'll share my screen with the bench csv in a sec but high level: our p50 is +10ms vs incumbent, p95 is -40ms, p99 is -120ms depending on batch. so mixed.
[00:30] Priya: wait you said p50 is higher? that sounds backward.
[00:34] Ravi: yeah sorry, clumsy phrasing—p50 is slightly higher for very small batches (1-2) because we did more safety checks, but the p95/p99 are better once the KV cash warms up.
[00:47] Maya: KV cash? do you mean KV cache? sometimes the transcripts make it funny.
[00:51] Ravi: right, KV cache. the warmup matters, and the incumbent has a big prefix cache warmed by a longer sustained load.

[01:10] Avery: let's look at the graphs — (screen) — so on slide one the red line is Redwood test, blue is IncumbentCloudAI baseline. p50 for single token completion is 42ms vs 34ms baseline, p95 238ms vs 282ms, p99 520ms vs 640ms.
[01:40] Jon: ok that's interesting — baseline is faster on small steady requests but they blow up on tails. what's causing your p50 delta?
[01:46] Ravi: a couple of things — kernel selection overhead when model context > 512, and our safety/jailed sandboxing step before tokens return. we can bypass some checks conditionally for trusted flows which should bring p50 in line.
[02:05] Priya: bypassing checks — we need to see audit trails, can you show how it's logged?
[02:12] Avery: yes, we'll provide the security appendix and the audit log pattern. it's an opt-in config; default stays strict.

[03:00] Maya: throughput — your report shows throughput plateau at ~250 req/s with 16-token avg. baseline does 300 stable. is that resource saturation?
[03:10] Ravi: part CPU/GPU scheduling and memory churn from KV cache eviction when sequences vary. when we bump batching aggressively we get better overall tokens/sec but higher tail latency for some requests.
[03:25] Jon: do you have the per-GPU utilization traces?
[03:28] Ravi: yes attached in the drive link — note that on the dedicated slot config we used 4xA100-simulated nodes, but the batch size policy limited to 8 per device to keep latency SLO.

[04:00] Avery: quick note — we purposely ran a mixed-workload test that included long context chats and short Q&A to mimic Calyx's production. that causes cache thrash. baseline tests were more homogeneous so it's a bit apples-to-oranges.
[04:20] Maya: fair point, but production is mixed so your mixed test is actually closer to our reality.

[05:00] Ravi: here's an interesting one: KV-cache hit rate jumps from 32% cold to 78% after 10 minutes sustained. the baseline's documentation suggests they run long-lived sessions which artificially improve tail. we've also instrumented cold-start traces — first 100 requests are where most p99 spikes happen.
[05:30] Priya: so warmup window matters. can you do a steady-state test for 2 hours?
[05:35] Ravi: yes we can schedule a sustained run, but we want to test scaling limits too.

[06:00] Avery: on quantization — we tested 8-bit and a 4-bit profile. 4-bit reduces tokens/sec cost by ~35% but increased hallucination risk on a couple of our eval prompts. we can tune the quantization tables per model.
[06:22] Jon: that hallucination bit is concerning. do you have examples?
[06:25] Ravi: yes, in the bench sheet there's a folder 'qual-evals' with prompt examples where entity copying was altered. those are edge cases; often it's due to aggressive group-wise quantization.

[07:00] Maya: ok from compliance side — SOC2, KMS, audit logs. you've given the appendix but need to confirm if KMS is customer-managed in private deploy.
[07:08] Avery: yes, private deploy supports customer KMS (HSM option) and the Private control plane adds audit-log forwarding — we'll include config snippets.

[08:00] Priya: anything about data residency? our EU tenants must stay in region.
[08:05] Avery: yes, we can pin region and have routing policy to keep requests in eu-west only. will include routing policy example.

[09:00] Ravi: moving back to perf, we tried two batch policies: conservative (max batch 8) and aggressive (max 32). conservative keeps p50 low but caps throughput. aggressive increases throughput to 340 req/s but p99 goes to 1.2s for small requests.
[09:25] Jon: that 1.2s p99 is unacceptable for UX. what's your recommendation?
[09:30] Ravi: for Calyx we recommend hybrid: small requests go to a low-latency pool (dedicated slots with reduced batching) and long context/throughput flows go to a throughput pool. smart routing can shift by header flags.
[09:45] Maya: cost-wise — how much extra is that?
[09:48] Avery: rough math: two small-latency dedicated slots ~ +12% monthly cost on top of baseline; throughput pool optimized with 4-bit quantization for bulk loads can cut token cost by 20-30%. detailed numbers in the shared sheet.

[10:30] Priya: lets talk about the throughput plateau — is it queue saturation on the RW side or the customer side?
[10:36] Ravi: our traces show the queuing happens inside the sharded runtime when many requests hit different KV prefixes causing cross-device syncs. baseline uses a different sharding that favors read locality but has worse tail on mixed loads.

[11:00] Maya: ok i'm worried about the tail behavior in peak windows for our clinicians. any mitigation besides hybrid pools?
[11:08] Ravi: yes — two mitigations: 1) prefix pinning (hold hot prefixes on a small set of GPUs to keep local hits) and 2) pre-warm synthetic traffic during shift changes. prefix pinning will reduce cold-cache p99 by ~40% in our sims.

[12:00] Jon: what are the operational risks of prefix pinning?
[12:05] Ravi: a little extra memory pressure and slightly lower overall utilization; but for critical prefixes it's worth it. pinning rules are policy-driven and reversible.

[13:00] Maya: can we see an operational runbook? how to failover if a pinned node dies?
[13:05] Avery: yes we'll send an ops runbook; failover is automatic with fallback to throughput pool and an incident playbook. we'll include estimated RTO/RPO.

[14:00] Priya: also curious about kernel selection — you mentioned context >512 triggers a slower kernel. can that be tweaked?
[14:08] Ravi: yes, depending on model we can choose a different attention kernel and precompile for the common context lengths. that reduces overhead for mid-sized contexts. we'll include a recommendations table.

[15:00] Avery: quick demo idea — if we provision two extra dedicated slots for next week's stress test we can show sustained 4-hour run with hybrid routing and pinning enabled.
[15:12] Maya: sounds good, can you do that on Tuesday morning (region aligned)?
[15:15] Avery: we'll aim for 2026-04-21 09:00 CET.

[16:00] Ravi: one more thing — we saw a specific request pattern where their frontend batches 5 rapid small requests which looks like 1 large. we can detect that at edge and split into the low-latency pool. will add a middleware suggestion.

[18:00] Jon: thanks, useful. what's the ask from our side this week?
[18:06] Avery: confirm stakeholders for the rollout decision, agree on the two-hour steady-state or 4-hour stress run, and accept the extra dedicated slots for the Tuesday test.

[19:00] Maya: i'll confirm by end of day tomorrow. Priya will sign off the security check once she sees the KMS appendix.

[20:00] Priya: quick question — competitor price was mentioned in your earlier email, can you send an apples-to-apples cost compare sheet?
[20:08] Avery: yes, i'll send an apples-to-apples cost sheet and the bench csv filtered for the critical workflows.

[21:00] (brief cross talk, link sharing)
[22:00] Ravi: note — there are a few noisy transcription artifacts in the raw file; i'll attach cleaned CSVs in the drive.

[23:00] Summary recap (Avery):
- p95/p99 are better overall vs incumbent but p50 needs minor tuning for tiny batches
- throughput plateau due to KV cache churn and sharding; mitigation: prefix pinning + hybrid pools
- quantization helps cost but must be validated for hallucination/quality
- next steps: send tuned latency CSV, schedule quantization deep-dive, provision dedicated slots for stress test

[24:00] Closing: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with dates and attachments.

End of transcript.
